title: Hartland Circuit (clockwise)
subtitle: SWCP Long Walkers · Friday 23 October 2026

stages.title: Stoke, Wargery and Kernstone Cross
stages.intro: The walk opens gently. After the briefing at the church and a look at St Nectan's Well, the lane heads south past Stoke Barton, drops to the river below Wargery and climbs to Kernstone Cross. Docton Mill and Milford lie about 600 m south of the route. Their stories are included below in case the group asks, but the lane down to them is unpleasant walking and the mill is closed, so the route stays on the higher ground.

stages.title: Down to Speke's Mill Mouth
stages.intro: From Kernstone Cross the lane runs west past Kernstone to the walk's highest point, about 116 m. The route then takes the footpath down the lower Milford Water valley to the coast at Speke's Mill Mouth, a drop of almost 80 m in under a kilometre.

stages.title: St Catherine's Tor to Hartland Quay
stages.intro: North of the waterfall the coast path runs along the floor of an old valley behind a line of headlands, then drops to Hartland Quay itself, the lowest point of the walk at about 16 m. Low water is at 10.38am (Clovelly times), so the reefs, wave-cut platforms and pier foundations should be well uncovered while the group is on this stretch.

stages.title: Rocket House, The Warren and Blackpool Mill
stages.intro: The climb out of the Quay to the Rocket House, about 55 m in 300 m, is the steepest pull so far. The path then crosses The Warren past the Pleasure House and Dyer's Lookout and drops to the Abbey River at Blackpool Mill for lunch. The hardest ground of the day comes straight after lunch, so let the group eat and rest properly.

stages.title: Berry Cliff, Blegberry and Smoothlands
stages.intro: This is the hardest section of the day. After lunch the path climbs over Berry Cliff, drops steeply to Blegberry Water, then climbs about 90 m onto Smoothlands. The steps are slippery when wet, so regroup at the top of each climb.

stages.title: Hartland Point
stages.intro: The path runs north along Blagdon Cliff to the Glenart Castle memorial, rounds the headland above the lighthouse past the old coastguard lookout, and comes down to the car park. This short stretch has the densest set of stories on the walk, so it is worth two stops: one at the memorial and one at the lookout.

stages.title: Farm lanes home to Stoke
stages.intro: The return is the easy stretch: nearly 4 km of green lanes and field paths across the plateau, about a kilometre back from the cliffs, past Blegberry and Berry and down through the Abbey valley. Expect mud after rain and stock in the fields. It is the best part of the day for conversation, and the farmhouses along it are older and more interesting than they look from the lane.

stops.name: St Nectan's Church
stops.talk: The tower behind us is 128 feet high, one of the tallest in Devon, and for centuries sailors used it as a landmark. The story goes that Gytha, mother of King Harold, founded a church here around 1050 in thanks for her husband Earl Godwin surviving a shipwreck. It is named after St Nectan, a Welsh hermit who, legend says, was beheaded by cattle thieves and carried his own head back to his spring. Foxgloves are said to have grown where his blood fell. His well is just down the lane, our first stop. Because of its size, locals call this the Cathedral of North Devon.
stops.background:
Background. The church is Grade I listed (Historic England 1333125). Most of the fabric is 14th and 15th century, restored around 1850 and again in 1910 and 1911. The highlights are the 15th-century rood screen, which runs the full width of the church in eleven bays, a late Norman font, wagon roofs, and a Catacleuse stone altar tomb moved here from Hartland Abbey in 1848. Historic England says the tower is "reputedly the tallest in Devon", while Explore Devon calls it the second highest, so "one of the tallest" is the safe phrase. The National Churches Trust and the North Devon Coast National Landscape both describe it as a long-standing landmark for shipping. The Godwin shipwreck story comes from the latter and is legend, not record.

The room over the north porch is traditionally known as the Pope's Chamber. Notes on the Hawker website say it is named after a local resident called Pope. It is reached by a steep, narrow stair and has a large fireplace, and the parish armour is thought to have been kept there in Elizabethan and Stuart times. Today it holds the parish stocks, Jacobean pulpit panels, medieval tiles and a 1613 list of who sat where. The Hartland Peninsula Association's coastal walk leaflet says finds from the chapel site on St Catherine's Tor, which we pass before lunch, are displayed there. If the group has five minutes inside, look for the 1922 window showing Gytha with Alfred the Great, William of Normandy and King Arthur, the 1530 pew ends carved "HP" for Hugh Prust (both from thornber.net), and two plaques to the publisher John Lane and his adopted heir Sir Allen Lane, founder of Penguin Books (National Churches Trust). The same source mentions a chair used by Emperor Haile Selassie when he opened the church fete, and a beam said to come from HMS Revenge. The Commonwealth War Graves Commission records eight First and Second World War casualties in the churchyard.

Hartland was a royal estate long before the church. In Domesday Book it was held by Countess Gytha in 1066 and by King William in 1086. It had 135 households, 700 sheep, 100 goats and 137 cattle, a large manor for Devon. St Nectan's Life survives in a 14th-century manuscript at Gotha. His feast is 17 June, when people still take foxgloves to the well (Wikipedia: Nectan of Hartland).

stops.name: St Nectan's Well
stops.talk: We start the day with St Nectan. This is his holy well, where he is supposed to have laid down his severed head. The little well-house is probably late medieval. Its water was used for baptisms in the church until fairly recently, and the last miracle claimed here was in the 1950s, though the Church didn't accept it. Every 17 June, his feast day, people still bring foxgloves.
stops.background: Background. Historic England (1146697) lists the well at Grade II and describes it as "probably late medieval but some reconstruction may have taken place". It has rubble walls, an ashlar front, a gabled roof, a pointed arched entrance on the east side and a slate shelf inside. The baptism and miracle details come from the Hartland Peninsula Association leaflet. It is signposted off the lane a short way from the church. The public toilets at Stoke are open 24 hours (Torridge District Council).

stops.name: Stoke Barton
stops.talk: The Abbey's largest remaining farm; farmhouse built for the improving tenant Exter.

stops.name: Wargery
stops.talk: Farm above the lane; the lane drops to the river here.

stops.name: Stoke Barton, Wargery and Kernstone Cross
stops.detail: 0.4 to 1.6 km, Kernstone Cross at SS 2368 2335
stops.talk: Kernstone was once a shared tenement. Several farmers worked intermixed strips and shared rights, medieval-style, until it was all merged into one farm. It had its own water mill, whose site is now lost, and possibly a chapel. Like most of the land we'll walk through today, it still belongs to the Abbey estate.
stops.background: Background. These details come from the Hartland Peninsula Association leaflet, a single source. I found nothing reliable on the names Kernstone or Wargery. Leaving Stoke, the lane passes Stoke Barton (0.4 km), which the same leaflet calls the Abbey's largest remaining farm. Its farmhouse was built for a tenant called Exter, an agricultural improver who experimented with fertilisers and an early threshing machine.

stops.name: Docton Mill
stops.detail: SS 2341 2274, about 600 m south of the route
stops.talk: Docton Mill is mentioned in a parish rate of 1682, and the site may be far older. It ground flour for Giffords, the Hartland bakers, until 1910. In the 1930s the owners rigged the waterwheel to make electricity, which mattered because this valley had no mains power until 1950. The generator still works. The gardens are lovely in season, but they closed on 5 October, so we're giving it a miss today.
stops.background: Background. Historic England (1104472) lists the mill at Grade II. It records some 17th-century fabric, the 1682 rate, a late 19th-century iron overshot wheel, machinery brought from Newton St Petrock mill in the late 1930s, and restoration in 1980. The mill's own history claims a Saxon origin, which I could not corroborate, and says the generator still produces about 5 kVA. The Docton family held the surrounding estate from the 15th century until the male line ended with Philip Docton in 1743 (Wikipedia: Docton). The Hartland Peninsula Association says the valley once had three water mills and the mansion of the richest man in 16th-century Hartland, probably a Docton.

stops.name: Kernstone
stops.talk: Former shared medieval tenement with its own mill and possibly a chapel; still part of the Abbey estate.

stops.name: Milford
stops.detail: hamlet at SS 2318 2263, about 600 m south of the route
stops.talk: Milford is in Domesday Book. In 1086 it had seven households, five villagers and two slaves, with land for three ploughs. Before the Conquest it belonged to a Saxon called Saewin. Twenty years later a Norman, Gosbert, held it. It was one of four Hartland manors, and aerial photographs still show the narrow medieval strip fields around it.
stops.background: Background. The figures come from Open Domesday. The tenant-in-chief in 1086 was Theobald son of Berner. The Hartland Peninsula Association leaflet adds the strip fields and says Milford had one of Stoke church's dependent chapels by the green, with remains visible until recently.

stops.name: The Milford Water valley
stops.talk: How fast is this coast disappearing? Sea level has been roughly where it is now for about 6,000 years. In that time the cliffs here have been retreating at something like two to four centimetres a year, up to about 240 metres in all. That's why the stream valleys we'll cross today all end in mid-air. Not everyone agrees on the full story, mind. One theory says ice at the edge of the last glaciation blocked and diverted these streams. Most geologists think the sea did the work.
stops.background: Background. The GCR report records that Milford Water has had "its left bank removed at four separate locations" by the sea. It reconstructs the former stream courses following Arber's 1911 study. It sets out the debate with Goudie and Gardner (1985), who proposed ice-margin blockage, and judges the ice idea less convincing because most of the valleys follow the grain of the rock. It also gives the retreat estimate of 20 to 40 mm a year.

stops.name: Longpeak and the Green Ranger
stops.detail: 580 m south of the path at about 2.6 km, SS 2224 2304
stops.talk: Just south of here, under Longpeak, two ships came to grief 72 years apart. In 1890 it was the Uppingham, the wreck that led to the Rocket House we'll pass above the Quay. In November 1962 the Royal Fleet Auxiliary tanker Green Ranger broke her tow in a Force 10 gale and went ashore with seven men aboard. The Hartland and Bude rescue teams fired rockets from the clifftop, but they fell short in a 70-mile-an-hour wind. So they waited for the tide to drop, carried the gear down onto the rocks and fired from there. All seven came ashore by breeches buoy in about an hour.
stops.background: Background. The RNLI journal records that on 17 November 1962 the tug Caswell was towing the tanker from Plymouth to Cardiff when the tow parted off Hartland Point. She went ashore "near Long Peak beach, three miles south of Hartland Point" in a northerly gale gusting to Force 10. HMS Agincourt found her by searchlight, and the Appledore coxswain Sidney Cann won the RNLI's silver medal. The shore rescue under George Read is described by the Bideford archive. The National Landscape notes a major operation to salvage scrap up the cliffs. Traces are still visible from the coast path at low tide, and relics are in the Hartland Quay museum and bar. We pass soon after low water (10.38am at Clovelly), so it is worth scanning the shore towards Longpeak for traces. The same page records the Liverpool barque Nepenthe, stranded at Milford Cliff in 1863 with four of her nine crew lost.

stops.name: Speke's Mill Mouth
stops.talk: This is the best coastal waterfall in Hartland, and geologists rate it among the finest in Britain. Milford Water's valley has been chopped off by the retreating cliff. So the stream drops over a vertical bed of hard sandstone, turns sharp left along the fold, then breaks through and drops again. The zigzags in the rock decide where the water goes. On the clifftop look for the old sand bins. Donkeys carried sand up from the beach in panniers, and farm tenancies even set how much sea sand each farmer could spread on his fields every year.
stops.background:
The falls. Heights vary by source. The National Landscape gives 15 m, while Geography South West gives the upper fall as 54 ft (about 16.5 m) in a series of four. A Geograph description counts five and puts it as dropping "down the dip of the rock and then turns sharply left along the strike". The Geography South West guide explains the mechanism. The upper fall crosses a near-vertical sandstone bed on the eastern limb of a tight syncline, then the stream turns along the fold and breaks out across an anticline. The GCR report calls it "the most spectacular" of the waterfalls on this coast, which it rates among the best in Britain. The common land around it is part of the SSSI.

The name and the mill. Nobody knows where "Speke's" comes from. The Hartland Peninsula Association and the National Landscape both mention a suggested link to the explorer John Hanning Speke, of Buckland Brewer, but say the evidence is hard to find. No mill at the mouth itself is recorded. The valley inland once held three water mills, and the Mills Archive gives Docton Mill, 600 m south of our route, the alternative name Spekes Valley Mill. The sand was carried up a zigzag path to open bins known as "sand lews".

stops.name: Mousse Le Moyec wreck (1940)
stops.talk: Free French collier aground December 1940; two steel bars stick up from the reef under St Catherine's Tor. Best at low tide.

stops.name: St Catherine's Tor
stops.talk: This 84-metre cone is the last surviving piece of the seaward side of that old valley. A chapel is said to have stood on top, probably belonging to the Abbey, and Victorian antiquarians found traces of a building, but erosion has since taken about 40 feet off the Tor. Behind it, in the marshy valley floor, the abbots kept a swan pool. You can still pick out their dam, a bank of clay faced with stone about 20 feet thick, running across the valley. And on the reef below, two steel bars sticking up out of the rock mark the wreck of a Free French collier lost here in December 1940.
stops.background:
Chapel and swannery. The National Landscape says "it is alleged that a chapel once stood on the top" and that erosion has removed the evidence. It quotes Dean Milles in 1760: "Catherine Tor, under which is a marsh in ye abbot's time a swan pool". It describes the "20ft thick, stone revetted clay dam" that "bisects the valley bottom". The Hartland Peninsula Association leaflet adds the antiquarian finds displayed in the Pope's Chamber, the 40 feet lost in a century, and recent surveys that found at least four shallow ponds at "Tor Marsh". You may hear that a Roman villa stood on the Tor. The SWCP Association and Geography South West say only that one is "believed" to have done, and I found no archaeological record to support it. Tell it as a tradition if at all.

The landform. Geography South West describes the Tor as conical, 84 m high and ringed by the old flood plain of Milford Water. Its seaward side is raw rock and its landward side smooth grass, a neat picture of what the sea is doing to it.

The Mousse Le Moyec. The Devon HER (MDV51976) records a Free French collier built at Lorient in 1921, sailing in ballast from Plymouth to Cardiff, which ran aground in December 1940. The site is marked by two steel bars standing up from the reef that runs out from under the Tor.

stops.name: Tor Marsh: the abbots' swan pool
stops.talk: Marshy valley floor behind the Tor where the abbots kept swans; a 20 ft thick stone-faced clay dam still crosses it. Position approximate.

stops.name: Childspit Beach and Wargery Water fall
stops.talk: Wargery Water follows part of an old coast-parallel valley and drops to the sea here, another hanging-valley waterfall.

stops.name: Screda Point and Childspit Beach
stops.talk: Notice we're walking along a flat valley floor with headlands between us and the sea. That flat-topped grassy headland, Screda Point, is the old seaward wall of a valley that used to run along the coast. The sea has broken through it in places. Down on the shore the rock stands up in steep walls and ribs, the folded beds cut off by the waves.
stops.background: Background. The Geography South West field guide describes Screda Point as the remnant seaward wall of an old valley that once ran from Speke's Mill past St Catherine's Tor to Hartland Quay. The GCR report notes that south of the Quay "buttress reefs are predominant", while north of it the platform bevels across all the beds. Wargery Water now follows part of that old valley and drops to the sea at Childspit Beach.

stops.name: The Stoke Warren standing stone
stops.detail: 4.2 km, SS 2250 2449, about 120 m off the path
stops.talk: Somewhere in the field above us is a standing stone about seven feet tall, probably prehistoric. Local folklore says it turns round whenever it hears the bells of Hartland church. Given how far the church is, it must have very good hearing.
stops.background: Background. The Devon Historic Environment Record (MDV7316) records a standing stone about 2.2 m high at Stoke Warren, "between St Catherine's Tor and Hartland Quay", at SS 2250 2450. It cites the archaeologist Leslie Grinsell (1976) for the bells story. I have not seen the stone myself and could not confirm it is visible from the path, so scan for it rather than promise it.

stops.name: 1860 timber ship wreck site
stops.talk: Unnamed 200-ton American timber ship lost 23 Jan 1860 between Shark's Teeth reef and the Quay; eight crew died. The Quay coastguard's first known callout.

stops.name: Hartland Quay
stops.detail: 4.5 km; slipway at SS 2221 2478, hotel beside the path
stops.talk: Hard to believe now, but this was a working port for 300 years. Tradition says Parliament authorised a quay here in 1566 with Raleigh, Drake and Hawkins as backers, but the first written record calls it 'Mr Abbott's Key', in 1602, after William Abbott of the Abbey, who built it. Ships brought in limestone, coal and timber from Wales and Bristol and took out corn and malt. Atlantic storms kept smashing the pier. When the railway reached Bideford in 1855 trade drained away, a storm breached the pier in 1887, and in 1896 the sea took the rest. The last trading ship left in 1893. The hotel was the merchant's house, malthouse and stores, and the bar is in the old stables. You can still see the stump of the pier wall and, at low tide, its foundation stones.
stops.background:
History. Historic England (1104452) lists the remains of the pier wall at Grade II. It credits the original pier to William Abbott, the first lay owner of the Abbey, and records that the first known reference, as "Mr Abbott's Key", dates from 1602 or 1603 (SWCP Association). After gale damage in 1841 the owner, Lewis William Buck, raised £1,200 for repairs. After the 1887 storm Sir George Stucley "refused to rebuild, merely re-facing the stump", and the rest was "swept away in 1896". The last trading ship, the Rosamund Jane, left in 1893. The hotel (Historic England 1166353) began in the early 18th century as a merchant's house with an adjoining malthouse, stables and stores. At one stage its central section held a bank, and it became a hotel in the late 19th century. Companies House shows the hotel partnership is controlled by members of the Stucley family, so the Quay is still part of the Abbey's world. On the slipway look for the 19th-century limekiln (National Landscape heritage leaflet). The present slipway was built in 1970 by the Hartland Boat Club.

Wrecks and wreckers. The hotel's history records the Hartland Quay coastguard's first known callout in January 1860. A Devon HER record matches it to an unnamed 200-ton American timber ship lost on 23 January 1860 between the Shark's Teeth reef and the Quay, with eight crew dead. Fifteen more vessels were wrecked here before 1900. The Wikipedia page on the Quay, citing North Devon and Lundy Shipwrecks, names the Edward and Ann (1809), Royal Saxon (1886), Londos (1891) and others. Someone will ask about wreckers. The National Landscape describes Hartland's "wreckers" as opportunists salvaging ships that were already lost, not people who lured them ashore. Cathryn Pearce's doctoral research found deliberate wrecking "not nearly as widespread" as legend claims, with the stereotype spread by newspapers and sermons and repeated by Victorian writers.

The rocks. This is the place for the geology talk, because the cliff behind the hotel is one of the classic sites in Britain for folded rocks. Stand on the slipway facing north. See Reading the rocks for the one-minute version and the detail behind it.

Coffee and facilities. On the day plan the group reaches the Quay at about 11.45am, so this is a comfort and coffee stop before lunch at Blackpool Mill. The Wreckers' Retreat is listed as open daily from 11am (CAMRA). The small shipwreck museum opens from Easter until October half term, 11am to 4pm (hotel history page), so it should still be open on the 23rd. Ring the hotel on 01237 441218 to confirm opening, whether it can take the group for coffee, and the museum. The Quay's toilets are in the former coastguard cottages, but I could not confirm they are open in late October. The Quay has also been a film set, for Treasure Island, Solomon Kane and the 2020 Rebecca.

stops.name: Hartland Quay Hotel and Wreckers' Retreat
stops.talk: Coffee stop at about 11.45. Bar listed as open from 11am. Shipwreck museum open until October half term. Phone 01237 441218.

stops.name: The Rocket House
stops.talk: In November 1890 the steamer Uppingham, carrying coal from Cardiff to Port Said, was driven onto the rocks under Longpeak, a couple of kilometres south of here, and eight of her crew died. Within three months the village had formed a Life Saving Apparatus Company and built this house for its rocket wagon. The rocket fired a line out to a stranded ship, the crew rigged a rope, and survivors came ashore one at a time in a breeches buoy, a canvas seat slung from the rope. Rocket teams on this coast kept going until helicopters took over in the 1980s. It's a private house now.
stops.background:
Background. The Hartland Quay Hotel's history page gives the Uppingham as a 2,203-ton steamer stranded "under Longpeak" on 23 November 1890, and says the company was formed and the house built within three months. That would put the building at the turn of 1890 and 1891. The SWCP Association gives 1890. The cargo and crew figures (eight lost of 28) come from Wikipedia's 1890 wreck list, and the eight dead are confirmed by local sources. That list places the wreck 4 nautical miles west of Hartland Point, which conflicts with "under Longpeak". Go with the local account. The National Landscape Hartland leaflet and the Geography South West Speke's Mill guide both say the rocket apparatus stayed in use until helicopters took over in the 1980s. It was designed by Henry Trengrouse, a Cornishman moved by the loss of HMS Anson at Loe Bar in 1807 (SWCP Association). The National Landscape records the building as a private dwelling and notes it on the 1904 OS map.

This is also the walk's closest point to Stoke, about 1 km by the field path to the churchyard. See Notes for walk leaders for using it as an escape route.

stops.name: Warren Beach
stops.talk: Faulting, a wide wave-cut platform and a natural arch. Old mouth of the stream now called Wargery Water.

stops.name: The Warren and the Pleasure House
stops.talk: This was a rabbit warren. Rabbits were farmed for meat and fur in artificial burrows, and that was a real rural industry until the late 1800s. The roofless ruin may have started as the warrener's house in the 1500s. By 1738 it was being called the Pleasure House, and the story goes that Paul Orchard of the Abbey, in the late 1700s, had that big arch made so he could back his carriage in and admire the view in comfort. It is now a Grade II listed folly.
stops.background:
Background. Historic England (1333133) describes the "Folly known as the Pleasure House" as "possibly late C16 in origin remodelled in later C18". It is square, roofless and built of rubble, with a large round-headed arch on the east side and traces of blocked windows, a fireplace and a stair. The listing records the name in a letter of 1738, shows the building on an early 18th-century estate map, and links its origin to the two William Abbotts of the later 16th century. The carriage story attaches to "the second Paul Orchard (1739 to 1812)". The National Landscape notes a recent community archaeology survey that looked for the warren itself, and that the 1988 film Paper House was shot on these cliffs. The Hartland Peninsula Association leaflet adds that the lifesaving crew practised on The Warren by firing rockets at a mast. That links neatly to the Rocket House we have just passed. A local suggestion that the ruin was a pirate lookout has no evidence behind it.

Below, Warren Beach shows faulting, a wide wave-cut platform and a natural arch (Geography South West). It is also where an older stream, the ancestor of today's Wargery Water, once reached the sea before cliff retreat cut it off (Geography South West, Hartland Quay to Speke's Mill).

stops.name: Dyer's Lookout
stops.talk: Look ahead, north along the cliffs. You can see the rock layers bent into great arches, and where the sea has eaten into those arches it leaves ridges like a hog's back. Right under us the beds stand on end, vertical, because they've been squeezed so hard. Nobody seems to know who Dyer was. The name has stuck to this viewpoint without any story attached, so if anyone in the group knows, I'd like to hear it.
stops.background: Background. The Marsland to Clovelly geology guide describes "large-scale antiformal folds" here that "are differentially eroded and form classic Hog's Back cliffs". The Geography South West guide notes the vertical beds at the Lookout. Neither the SWCP Association, the National Landscape nor the Abbey gives an origin for the name.

stops.name: Abbey Gazebo
stops.talk: 19th-century gazebo on the cliff, reached by a zigzag path from the Abbey. Restored 2004. 200 m inland.

stops.name: Blackpool Mill and the Abbey River: lunch stop
stops.talk: This cottage was the Abbey's corn mill, where the estate's grain was ground, for a fee. The beach earned its keep too. Sand went up the valley on donkeys and was sold to farmers to lighten their heavy clay, and seaweed gathered at low tide was spread as fertiliser. It was still working in the 19th century. Since then it has had a second career on screen. It was the Dashwoods' Barton Cottage in the BBC's Sense and Sensibility, and it appears in The Shell Seekers and The Night Manager. The stream beside it is the Abbey River, which we cross again near the Abbey on the way home. It is Hartland's longest river, and it ends here in a valley left hanging above the beach.
stops.background:
Background. The Hartland Abbey estate says the cottage "was originally the site of the estate's corn mill". It later housed two farm workers and became a holiday let in the 20th century. The National Landscape dates the mill to at least the 16th century. It notes an 1807 record of the miller's charges, the mill on the 1864 Ordnance Survey map, and working probably until the end of the 19th century. The estate's cottage sheet calls it 15th century and records The Shell Seekers in 2005 and Sense and Sensibility in May 2007. The 2019 version adds The Night Manager in 2015. The National Landscape Hartland leaflet adds that sand from this beach was carried up the valley by donkey and sold to farmers to improve their heavy clay, and that seaweed was gathered at low tide as fertiliser. The building is not listed, so don't confuse it with the listed Blackpool Mill in Pembrokeshire. At about 15 m, the river crossing here is, with the Quay, the lowest point of the walk.

The Geography South West field guide describes the Abbey River as the parish's longest, rising near an Iron Age hillfort close to Clovelly. The GCR report notes that its flat floor hangs only about 12 m above the beach. It has cut its final gorge through ice-age rubble, stony clay that crept downslope in freeze-thaw conditions during the last glaciation, rather than through bedrock. That is why this valley mouth is gentler than the sheer drops at Blegberry and Speke's Mill.

About 200 m inland, on the cliff at SS 2288 2546, the Abbey's 19th-century Gazebo sits at the top of a zigzag path from the house. It was restored in traditional materials in 2004 and is now used for weddings. Look back up the valley side for it as you cross the river.

stops.name: Berry Cliff
stops.talk: On a fine summer's day in 1879, a French lugger carrying pit props to Cardiff ran aground below this cliff. Her captain had mistaken the Hartland Point light for a Welsh one, and he was so convinced the locals would strip his boat that he refused to trust the coastguard. It took the vicar's wife, who spoke French, to persuade him that nobody here was going to plunder his ship.
stops.background: Background. The story is told in the National Landscape Hartland leaflet. It makes a good postscript to the wrecker question raised at Hartland Quay. The captain's fear reflects a reputation that historians now think was largely exaggerated.

stops.name: Damehole Point
stops.detail: 6.9 km, SS 2222 2628, 200 m west of the path at Blegberry
stops.talk: The reef running out from Damehole Point has wrecked at least three ships, two of them within a year of each other. In 1887 the schooner Star of Peace was smashed to pieces on it, and the next year a ship carrying 1,300 tons of iron ore was lost on the same rocks. Both crews got away in their own boats. Every one of those sandstone ribs you can see running out to sea is a ship-killer at half tide.
stops.background: Background. The wreck details come from the National Landscape Hartland leaflet. The GCR report notes a spring-fed stream dropping 22 m over the cliff on the north side of the Point. I found nothing reliable on the meaning of the name Damehole.

stops.name: Blegberry Water and beach
stops.talk: Along with the Quay and the Blackpool Mill crossing, this is one of the lowest points of the day. Blegberry Water drops over a sheer rock step onto the beach, a classic example of the hanging-valley waterfalls on this coast. The stream never managed to cut down to sea level, so it falls straight off the end of its valley, and you saw the same thing on a grander scale at Speke's Mill this morning.
stops.background: Background. The GCR report cites the geologist Arber, who in 1911 called this a "primary sheer waterfall", falling from about 35 m above sea level down a joint in the rock. The National Landscape leaflet says an anchor from the French ship Hoche, which foundered in 1882, can be seen on the beach by Damehole Point. I could not verify this, so present it as "said to be there" if anyone goes down to look. The beach is a short detour from the path. On 23 October the tide will be rising through the early afternoon, so allow for a narrowing beach if anyone takes it.

stops.name: Smoothlands
stops.talk: Look down at this flat-bottomed valley. No river runs along it now. It was once the lower course of a stream running parallel to the coast, joined by others from north and south. The cliffs have been retreating inland faster than the streams could cut down, and the sea has bitten through the valley at both ends. What is left is a valley floor hanging in the air, with the streams now tipping straight over the cliff as waterfalls. We've seen the same thing several times today, most dramatically at Speke's Mill Mouth this morning.
stops.background: Background. The GCR site report for the Hartland coast describes Titchberry Water falling over the northernmost waterfall, where the cliffs drop to just over 30 m. Its flat valley floor continues south between the small hill called Smoothlands and the valley side. The BGS memoir for Bideford and Lundy explains that the Abbey stream "was once joined by the Titchberry Water from the north and the Milford Water from the south". The "eastward recession of the cliff line has destroyed the lower reaches of this system". The SWCP Association adds two human details. Scrub on the valley floor marks a large medieval fishpond, and the lone caravan there predates the area's protected landscape designation.

stops.name: HMHS Glenart Castle memorial
stops.talk: This stone remembers a hospital ship. At ten to four in the morning on 26 February 1918, the Glenart Castle was steaming from Newport to France to collect wounded soldiers. She was lit up and marked with red crosses, as the rules of war required. A German submarine, UC-56, torpedoed her about 20 miles out there to the west-north-west. Around 160 people died, including eight nurses. The memorial was put up in 2002, and the British Legion still holds a service here every 26 February.
stops.background: Background. The ship left Newport on 25 February 1918 bound for Brest to collect wounded Portuguese soldiers (North Devon Gazette). The number lost varies by source. The SWCP Association and the National Landscape give 162 dead (the National Landscape adds that eight were nurses), while Wikipedia gives 153 lost of 182 aboard. The Gazette says the exact figure is lost to history, so "around 160" is fair. The U-boat's commander, Kapitänleutnant Wilhelm Kiesewetter, was held in the Tower of London after the war but released and never tried. The IWM memorial record describes a rough-hewn stone with a black granite tablet, dedicated on 26 February 2002, the 84th anniversary. It names the master, Lieutenant Commander Burt, and the matron, Katy Beaufoy, and states that "the ship lies 20 miles WNW from this stone". Two months later, on 18 April 1918, the collier Gregynog was torpedoed by UB-86 about 16 miles south-west of the Point, with three lives lost (uboat.net). It is a reminder that these approaches were a hunting ground in both wars.

stops.name: The wreck of the Johanna
stops.detail: below the Point, best seen from 8.8 to 9.0 km
stops.talk: On New Year's Eve 1982 a small Dutch-owned cargo ship, the Johanna, carrying wheat to Cardiff, was driven onto the rocks in a gale less than 400 metres from the lighthouse. An RAF helicopter from Chivenor lifted off four of the crew and the Clovelly lifeboat took the other three. Nobody died. By the next year the hull had broken in two, and the sea has been taking her apart ever since. See if you can spot any rusting remains on the rocks.
stops.background: Background. The SWCP Association and a Geograph photo record give her as Panama-registered and Dutch-owned, bound from the Netherlands to Cardiff. Sources disagree on how much is still visible. The SWCP page describes rusted remains on the rocks, but a 2022 geography field guide says very little is left. Set expectations accordingly.

stops.name: The lookout: Lundy, the Promontory of Hercules and the lighthouse
stops.talk: This corner is where the Bristol Channel meets the open Atlantic, and it has been a landmark for a very long time. The Greek geographer Ptolemy, writing in the second century, marked a 'Promontory of Hercules' on his map of Britain, and it is generally taken to be this headland. Below us is the lighthouse, built in 1874 and lit by Lady Stucley from the Abbey. It stopped shining in 2012, and in 2022 its historic lantern, one of only three like it in the world and valued at about a million pounds, was stolen from a store in Ilfracombe. Out to the north-north-west is Lundy, 11 miles off. Its granite is only about 60 million years old, a baby compared with the 320-million-year-old rock under our feet.
stops.background:
The headland. Ptolemy's Herculis promontorium is identified "all but universally" with Hartland Point (Dartmoor walks article), although his western longitudes are badly out (Saxon History), so "generally identified" is the honest wording. The lookout itself is no longer manned and now houses electronic surveillance equipment (SWCP Association). Geologically, Hartland Point is a nationally important site for its folds (North Devon RIGS audit); see Reading the rocks below for how to explain them.

The lighthouse. Historic England (1309148) records that work on the access road began in 1871 and the foundation stone was laid in November 1872, with a sealed bottle of names, newspapers and coins set into the wall. Lady Stucley lit it on 1 July 1874. Trinity House credits the design to its Engineer-in-Chief, Sir James Douglass. Waves kept undermining the rock shelf, so a sea wall 30 m long and 6 m high was added in 1925. The station was automated in 1984, and the keepers' houses were demolished to make a helipad. Since 2012 the light has come from a small separate structure, an LED 20.5 m above high water with a range of 8 nautical miles (SWCP Association). The tower has since been sold privately. Crimestoppers reported the January 2022 theft of the lantern, which was in storage awaiting refurbishment. The access road is closed because of frequent rockfalls.

Lundy. The island lies about 18 km (11 miles) out. Its granite has been dated to about 57 to 60 million years ago (Charles et al. 2017; Lisica et al. 2025), from the same burst of volcanic activity that built Skye and Mull. Its waters have a long protection record (Lundy MCZ): a voluntary marine reserve in 1971, a statutory Marine Nature Reserve in 1986, a No Take Zone in 2003 and England's first Marine Conservation Zone in 2010. For a rogue to go with the view, the National Landscape leaflet tells the story of Thomas Benson, an 18th-century MP for Barnstaple. He used Lundy as a base for smuggling and kept convicts there as forced labour when he was supposed to be transporting them to America. He scuttled a ship for the insurance money, and when that came out his captain was hanged and Benson fled to Portugal.

This is also the best place on the walk to scan the sea for birds. See Wildlife and plants for what to expect in late October.

stops.name: Hartland Point Lighthouse (below)
stops.talk: 1874, Sir James Douglass; lit by Lady Stucley. Discontinued 2012; lantern stolen 2022. No public access.

stops.name: Barley Bay
stops.talk: Bay below the car park on the north side of Hartland Point, where the Bristol Channel coast begins.

stops.name: Hartland Point car park, café and radar station
stops.detail: 9.3 km; car park SS 2348 2746, radar dome 300 m east
stops.talk: The white dome on the skyline has been listening to the sky since the Second World War. In 1941 it was a naval station intercepting German radio for the codebreakers at Bletchley Park. It then became a low-level radar station tracking ships and aircraft, and in the Cold War a fighter control centre ready to direct RAF interceptors against Soviet bombers. The old station closed in 1987. The dome you see now is a civil air-traffic radar, feeding the national control centre at Swanwick in Hampshire.
stops.background:
Background. Subterranea Britannica gives the fullest history. The Army ran a coast defence radar here early in the war, and on 7 June 1942 the RAF took it over as Chain Home Low station 19A. In the early 1950s it was rebuilt as a ground-controlled interception station under the ROTOR programme and became 405 Signals Unit in June 1953. Its fighter control role ended in 1958, though range-safety radar continued into the 1980s and a nuclear reporting cell worked here until about 1975. The SWCP Association dates the fighter control role from 1955, so expect small differences between sources.

The refreshment kiosk by the car park (Hartland Point Refreshments, 07771 590083) sells coffee, tea and light snacks, but its late-October opening could not be confirmed. There are no toilets here. On the day plan this is around 1.30pm, a natural short break before the lanes home. From the car park, look down into Barley Bay on the north side of the Point, then east along the cliffs to Shipload Bay, about 1 km away. Shipload Bay is a geological site in its own right, where Bude Formation sandstones lie on the limb of a fold running from Hartland Point (GCR: Shipload Bay).

stops.name: Hartland Point radar station
stops.talk: 1941 naval Y station for Bletchley Park, then Chain Home Low, Cold War ROTOR fighter control. Now a civil air-traffic radar.

stops.name: Shipload Bay (view east)
stops.talk: Bay about 1 km east of the car park; Bude Formation sandstones on the limb of a syncline. Seen from the Point, not visited.

stops.name: Blagdon Farm and the Lundy helipad
stops.talk: This working farm doubles as Lundy's winter airport. From November to March the supply ship can't run, so a helicopter flies from that field to the island in about seven minutes, on Mondays and Fridays. This year's flights start next Monday, 26 October, so we're a few days too early to see one.
stops.background: Background. The Landmark Trust runs the winter helicopter from 26 October 2026 to 2 January 2027 and again from 25 January to 22 March 2027. The summer ship MS Oldenburg sails until the end of October. The SWCP Association asks walkers to respect Blagdon as a working farm.

stops.name: Blegberry Farm
stops.detail: 11.0 km, SS 2320 2622, 50 m off the path
stops.talk: Blegberry is a farmhouse with gun loopholes in its walls. The Atkyns family built it in the early 1600s, and you can still read their dates on the building: 1606 on the courtyard wall, 1627 over a fireplace, 1657 on the well-house. Why would a farmer need gunports? Pirates were a real threat on this coast in the 1600s, and the house may also have been fortified during the Civil War. One local story says William Atkyns was a Royalist who collected the hated Ship Money tax, which would have given him plenty of reasons to bolt the door.
stops.background: Background. Historic England (1104470) lists the farmhouse at Grade II, with a plaster overmantel dated 1627 and initialled "WMA" for William and Margery Atkyns, who married in 1623. The well-house 130 m to the west is inscribed "1657 WA", and the U-shaped farm range is listed too. The Gatehouse gazetteer classes Blegberry as a probable fortified farmhouse with gun loopholes. It also raises, more speculatively, that this may be the site of a lost castle licensed to the Dinham family in 1201, based only on nearby "castle" field names. The Ship Money story and a claim that the name comes from a hillfort called "Black Bury", since lost to the sea, both come from a single National Landscape leaflet, so tell them as local tradition.

stops.name: Blegberry well-house (1657)
stops.talk: Grade II well-head inscribed 1657 WA for William Atkyns, 130 m west of Blegberry farmhouse.

stops.name: Berry and Markadon
stops.detail: 12.0 km; Berry at SS 2344 2530 beside the path, Markadon 290 m east
stops.talk: The farmhouse we are passing is Berry. It looks like an ordinary Devon farm, but in the 18th century it was a house of some quality, home to the Wolferstans, a gentry family, and the back wing still has a dovecote built into it, with nesting holes for pigeons. Keeping doves was a privilege of the better-off, and they were fresh meat in winter. An illustration of the Abbey from 1767 shows Berry in the distance.
stops.background: Background. Berry Farmhouse is Grade II listed. The listing describes an early to mid 18th-century remodelling of an older house with 17th-century fabric at the rear, a columbarium (the dovecote) in the rear wing, and calls it an "unusual, unaltered survival". Markadon Farmhouse, across the fields to the east, is older still. It is a 17th-century, possibly late-medieval, three-room-and-cross-passage house with a stone spiral stair, perhaps built around an open hall. I found nothing reliable on the place-name Berry, so avoid the tempting "burh means fort" explanation unless someone in the group knows better.

stops.name: Markadon Farmhouse
stops.talk: Grade II. 17th-century, possibly late-medieval cross-passage house with a stone spiral stair. 290 m east.

stops.name: Abbey summer house
stops.talk: Estate garden building beside the path. Abbey woodland gardens, Ladies' Walk c.1750, Jekyll bog garden nearby.

stops.name: Hartland Abbey and its grounds
stops.detail: 12.4 to 12.6 km; Abbey at SS 2405 2490, 240 m off the path
stops.talk: Through the trees to the east is Hartland Abbey. Augustinian canons lived here from the 12th century until February 1539, when the last abbot, Thomas Pope, surrendered it to Henry VIII. Henry gave it to William Abbott, the Sergeant of his Wine Cellar, and it has passed down through the family ever since, through three heiresses. The Stucleys still live there. You may know it from television. Sense and Sensibility, The Night Manager and House of the Dragon were all filmed on the estate, and we ate our lunch beside the Sense and Sensibility cottage at Blackpool Mill.
stops.background:
Background. The Abbey's own history gives it as built in 1157 and consecrated in 1160. Historic England's Grade I listing gives a foundation of about 1175 and dates the grant to William Abbott to 1546. The house was remodelled in Gothick style in 1779 by John Meadows, with later work by George Gilbert Scott in 1862. The Abbey describes itself as the last monastery in England to be dissolved. The official record (Letters and Papers of Henry VIII) shows Hartland surrendered on 22 February 1539, signed by Abbot Thomas Pope, who received a £60 pension. Waltham Abbey held out until 23 March 1540 and is usually given as the last. "Among the last" is the accurate version. The estate passed by marriage from the Abbotts to the Luttrells of Dunster Castle in 1583, to Paul Orchard in the early 18th century, and to George Buck in 1812. His descendant took the name Stucley in 1859 on being made a baronet.

The path down from Berry to the Abbey River skirts the Abbey's woodland gardens. Parks and Gardens UK dates Ladies' Walk, which linked the woodland to the three walled gardens, to planting around 1750. Gertrude Jekyll, a house guest, laid out the Bog Garden and Fernery in the early 20th century. Both were lost and then rediscovered in 1996. The estate restored a Woodland Summerhouse in 2011, where Lady Winifred Fortescue wrote during the war after escaping Vichy France. OpenStreetMap marks a summer house right beside our path at 12.4 km (SS 2371 2504). I could not confirm whether this is that building, so present it as one of the estate's garden buildings.

The Abbey and gardens are closed on the day. The 2026 season ran from 29 March to 1 October, Sundays to Thursdays only (hartlandabbey.com).

From the valley floor the route climbs about 50 m back up to Stoke, the last pull of the day, and the walk ends at the church at around 3pm.

stops.name: Finish: Stoke church car park
stops.talk: Limited parking by the church. Stoke public toilets are listed as open 24 hours.

dayplan.label: Meet and walk briefing, St Nectan's Church
Kernstone Cross, lane and path to the coast

leader.title: Notes for walk leaders
leader.html:
Weather, daylight and tide

Sunset on Friday 23 October is 6.08pm, with civil twilight until about 6.43pm. The clocks go back two days later, on Sunday 25 October (Royal Museums Greenwich). The day plan finishes at 3pm, leaving three hours of daylight in hand. Tides at Clovelly, the nearest published station, are low water 10.38am (2.1 m) and high water 4.40pm (7.5 m) (tidetimes.org.uk). Hartland Quay will be close to this but not identical. Going clockwise puts Speke's Mill and the Quay around low water, which is ideal for the reefs, the pier foundations and any Green Ranger traces at Longpeak. The tide then rises through the afternoon, building towards spring tides after the full moon on 26 October, so a beach detour at Blegberry after lunch needs care. On 17 October the Met Office forecast for the day was heavy showers, 15°C, and gusts up to 44 mph (Met Office, Hartland Quay). That is six days out and will change, but it is worth checking on Wednesday evening and again on the morning.

Short cuts and escape routes

There are two good ways back to Stoke from the coast. From the Rocket House (4.9 km), a field path runs parallel to the road to Stoke churchyard, about 1 km (SWCP Association), which cuts the day to about 6 km. From Blackpool Mill (6.0 km), the path inland along the Abbey River leads up the wooded valley to the road below St Nectan's Church (SWCP Association, Dyer's Lookout walk). That makes lunch the natural point to decide who carries on over the hardest section of the day. Between Blegberry and Hartland Point there is no easy exit, and from the Point the lanes home are the route itself. In strong westerlies, the clifftop between Smoothlands and the lookout is the most exposed stretch.

Ground and hazards

  • Steep steps and slopes. The hardest ground is between the Quay and Smoothlands (4.6 to 8.1 km), with long flights of steps and short steep pitches that are slippery when wet. Regroup at the top of each climb.
  • The descent to Speke's Mill and the Quay. The path drops almost 80 m to Speke's Mill Mouth and then descends to the Quay slipway. Both are steep, and the climb from the Quay to the Rocket House straight after is the sharpest of the morning.
  • Unfenced cliffs and rockfall. Keep the group back from the edge, especially above the lighthouse, where the access road is closed because of frequent rockfalls.
  • Mud. The green lanes on the return are likely to be very wet after a showery week.
  • Wind. Hartland Point takes the full force of westerly weather. Gusts in the forecast range make the clifftop edge a real hazard, so walk well inland of it.
  • Livestock and stiles. Expect stock in the inland fields and several stiles. Keep dogs on leads near animals and the cliff edge.
  • Seals. If a seal or pup is on a beach, stay at least 100 m away and keep dogs on leads. See Wildlife and plants.

What is open on the day

Place Status on Friday 23 October Source
Stoke public toilets Listed as open 24 hours Torridge District Council
Hartland Point refreshment kiosk Unconfirmed, ring 07771 590083 Hartland Point Refreshments
Wreckers' Retreat, Hartland Quay Listed as open daily from 11am; ring 01237 441218 to confirm food and group size CAMRA
Hartland Quay shipwreck museum Open Easter to October half term, 11am to 4pm, so probably open Hartland Quay Hotel
Hartland Quay toilets In the old coastguard cottages; late-October opening unconfirmed Wikipedia
Hartland Abbey and gardens Closed (season ended 1 October) Hartland Abbey
Docton Mill gardens and tea room Closed (season ended 5 October) Docton Mill
Lundy helicopter No flights (winter service starts 26 October) Landmark Trust

Parking at Stoke is limited (SWCP Association), so encourage car sharing. Hartland Quay car park (EX39 6DU) is the fallback.

Emergencies

On the cliffs or the shore, dial 999 and ask for the Coastguard. Elsewhere, ask for ambulance. Give the nearest grid reference from the points of interest table. Mobile signal is unreliable in the deep valleys at Blegberry, the Abbey River and Speke's Mill, so move up to open ground before calling. The nearest A&E is North Devon District Hospital, Raleigh Park, Barnstaple EX31 4JB (01271 322577), roughly 35 to 45 minutes' drive (Royal Devon). Bideford Minor Injuries Unit is closed (Royal Devon), so for minor injuries use NHS 111 or the Torrington or Holsworthy services. For a seal or other marine animal in trouble, call BDMLR on 01825 765546.

leader.title: Reading the rocks
leader.html:
The best place to give this talk is the slipway at Hartland Quay, facing north towards the cliff behind the hotel. The same story explains Smoothlands, Blegberry, St Catherine's Tor and Speke's Mill, so it is worth landing it well once.

Talking point (one minute, at Hartland Quay). "Look at the cliff. The pale bands are sandstone and the dark bands are mudstone. About 320 million years ago they were laid down flat, layer on layer, on the floor of a great basin, each sand layer dumped in minutes by an underwater avalanche of sediment. Then two continents collided to make the supercontinent Pangaea, and this basin was crushed from the south. Hard sandstone and soft mudstone together buckle into these sharp zigzags, called chevron folds. The ribs running out across the beach are the same folds, planed flat by the waves. They are the reefs that wrecked so many of the ships we've talked about today."

The rocks

The cliffs are interbedded grey sandstones and dark mudstones of Upper Carboniferous age, about 320 million years old. They were laid down in the Culm Basin, a basin in front of the rising Variscan mountain belt (Geological Society: Hartland Quay). The sandstones are turbidites. Each bed has a sharp base, grades finer upwards and carries groove and ripple casts on its underside, the scour marks of the current that laid it.

Two formations meet on this coast. The older Crackington Formation is rhythmic dark mudstone with thin turbidite sandstones (BGS Lexicon: Crackington). The younger Bude Formation is thicker grey sandstone with black shales (BGS Lexicon: Bude). The official boundary is the top of the Hartland Quay Shale, a black mudstone 1.47 m thick exposed at the Quay itself. It contains torpedo-shaped fossil fish droppings and occasional crushed goniatites, the coiled shells used to date these rocks (North Devon RIGS audit). In practice geologists draw the line at the first massive Bude-type sandstone.

There is a genuine argument about where these rocks formed. The Geological Society describes deep-marine turbidites. The British Geological Survey says the Bude Formation accumulated in "a large-scale freshwater lake situated on a broad shelf" with occasional marine incursions, and others have argued for a brackish delta or a submarine fan (GCR: Bude Coast). Horseshoe-crab trails in the Bude Formation are one reason for doubting a deep-sea origin. Popular guides often say "brackish sea". If a geologist in the group pushes, "the experts still disagree" is the honest answer.

The folds

The Variscan Orogeny, the collision that assembled Pangaea about 300 million years ago, buckled the layers into upright, sometimes slightly overturned, chevron folds with an east-west trend (RIGS audit; GCR Hartland Quay). Chevrons form where weak mudstone alternates with stiff sandstone. Deformation weakens northwards away from the mountain front, so the folding here is a little gentler than at Millook in Cornwall (Deposits magazine). Hartland Point is a Geological Conservation Review site for its folds, and the coast is crossed by north-west to south-east faults.

The hanging valleys and waterfalls

The GCR report rates the Hartland coastal waterfalls among the best in Britain. Its site runs about 6 km from Longpeak to Hartland Point. The cliffs have retreated faster than the streams can cut down, so valleys are left hanging and the streams drop over the edge, at Smoothlands, Damehole, Blegberry and Speke's Mill. Where a valley ran parallel to the coast, as from Speke's Mill to the Quay, the sea has broken through its seaward wall and left headlands such as Screda Point and St Catherine's Tor. The Abbey River is the exception. It hangs only about 12 m above the beach because it cut its last stretch through soft ice-age rubble.

The shore platforms

Wave-cut platforms up to 300 m wide are cut into the folded rock. North of the Quay they bevel across every bed, while to the south the hard sandstone stands up as steep walls and buttress reefs. The tidal range is large. On 23 October the Clovelly tide runs from 2.1 m at 10.38am to 7.5 m at 4.40pm, a range of more than 5 m, so the reefs appear and vanish through the day.

Glossary

  • Turbidite. A sand layer dumped by an underwater avalanche of sediment, coarse at the bottom and finer upwards.
  • Chevron fold. A zigzag fold with straight sides and sharp hinges, typical where hard and soft layers alternate.
  • Variscan Orogeny. The mountain-building collision about 300 million years ago that formed Pangaea and folded these rocks.
  • Goniatite. An early coiled relative of the ammonites, used to date the black shales.
  • Hanging valley. A valley whose lower end has been cut away by cliff retreat, so its stream drops over the cliff.
  • Wave-cut platform. The near-flat rock surface between the tides, planed off by the waves.
  • Head. Stony clay that crept downslope under freeze-thaw conditions in the ice age.
  • Strike and dip. Strike is the direction a tilted layer runs along the ground; dip is the direction and angle it slopes down.

leader.title: Wildlife in late October
leader.html:
Talking point (one minute). "Everything from the cliff edge to the high-tide line here is protected twice over. The land is part of the Marsland to Clovelly Coast SSSI and a European Special Area of Conservation for its sea cliffs, heath and stunted oak woods. The sea is the Hartland Point to Tintagel Marine Conservation Zone. Lundy, on the horizon, was England's first MCZ in 2010. Late October is grey seal pupping time, so if we see a seal on a beach we keep well back and keep our voices down."

Birds

Hartland Point is the best place on the route to stop and scan the sea. The SWCP Association rates autumn as the best season there, especially on windy days, for skuas, terns and shearwaters and the occasional unusual gull. Be realistic about the date, though. Further down the South West coast, the peak passage of Balearic shearwaters and skuas comes from late September to early October (BirdGuides SeaWatch SW summary), and Manx shearwaters have left for South America by then (RSPB). By 23 October, anything passing is a bonus that depends on the weather. A westerly blow on the day improves the odds.

The resident cast is more reliable. The SWCP Association's Speke's Mill walk notes peregrines and kestrels hunting over the clifftop grassland, and ravens are a near-certainty along the cliffs. Late October is also the peak of thrush and finch movement through Lundy (Lundy Field Society), so flocks of redwings and fieldfares arriving over the clifftop fields would be in keeping. Hartland Point is also known as a good winter site for red-throated diver (Birding Places).

Choughs will probably come up as a question, because they are spreading along the north Cornish coast. The North Devon Coast chough report lists Hartland Point as a historic breeding area. The last Devon breeding was near Lynton in 1910, and none of the recent north Devon sightings it lists are at Hartland. A chough here would be worth reporting.

Grey seals

Pupping on this coast runs from August to December and peaks in October (SWCP Association with Cornwall Seal Group). I found no documented pupping beaches on the Hartland mainland, but a white-coated pup on any cove should be treated as sensitive. The guidance is to stay at least 100 m away, keep dogs on leads, stay quiet and out of sight, and never approach. The Defra and Seal Alliance Give Seals Space campaign has a simple rule: if a seal is looking at you, you have already disturbed it. Report a pup that looks injured or abandoned to the BDMLR hotline on 01825 765546.

Dolphins and porpoises

Harbour porpoises are seen around Lundy all year and common dolphins mostly from April to October (Lundy Field Society). From the Point or The Warren, a calm patch of sea is worth a minute's watching.

Plants and habitats

The clifftops are a patchwork of maritime grassland, heath and scrub (North Devon Coast landscape assessment). The JNCC description of the Special Area of Conservation highlights the oak woods in the coastal valleys, wind-pruned so hard they are sometimes barely taller than the heather, and the abundance of hay-scented buckler-fern, a fern of mild, wet Atlantic coasts. Crush a frond in the Abbey or Milford valleys and it smells faintly of new-mown hay. Western gorse flowers from late summer, so some yellow should still be showing on the heath. In the wooded valleys at the start and end of the walk, late October is fungus season. I could not find a local species list, so treat finds there as a chance for the group's naturalists to shine.

Two bigger designations frame all of this. The coast lies in the North Devon Coast National Landscape, an AONB since 1960 and renamed in 2023. It also sits within the North Devon UNESCO Biosphere Reserve, which in 2002 became the UK's first "new style" biosphere.

leader.title: Route at a glance
leader.html:
The walk is a 13.2 km clockwise loop that starts and finishes at St Nectan's Church, Stoke (around SS 235 247), with 600 m of climbing (OS Maps route). OS Maps rates it Difficult. On the day plan below, a 10am start finishes at Stoke around 3pm.

The route runs in three parts. The first 2.9 km go south by lane past Stoke Barton, Wargery and Kernstone, then down the lower Milford Water valley to the coast at Speke's Mill Mouth. From there the route follows the South West Coast Path north for about 6 km, past St Catherine's Tor, down to Hartland Quay itself, over The Warren to Blackpool Mill, and on past Blegberry and Smoothlands to Hartland Point. It returns south by green lanes and field paths past Blagdon, Blegberry and Berry, through the Abbey valley to Stoke. Docton Mill and Milford are no longer on the route, but their stories are kept in Stage 1 because they are only about 600 m away.

The height never goes above about 120 m, but the coast path is a constant run of short, steep valleys. The lowest points are Hartland Quay and the Abbey River crossing at Blackpool Mill, both about 15 to 16 m. Most of the climbing comes between the Quay and Smoothlands.

Stretch km Climb Descent
Stoke, Wargery and Kernstone to the lane's high point 0.0 to 2.1 67 m 38 m
Down the Milford Water valley to Speke's Mill Mouth 2.1 to 3.0 0 m 77 m
Speke's Mill, St Catherine's Tor and down to Hartland Quay 3.0 to 4.6 77 m 88 m
Hartland Quay up to the Rocket House 4.6 to 4.9 55 m 0 m
The Warren, Dyer's Lookout and Blackpool Mill to Berry Cliff 4.9 to 6.2 53 m 83 m
Berry Cliff down to Blegberry Water 6.2 to 7.0 59 m 97 m
Blegberry Water up to Smoothlands 7.0 to 8.1 90 m 34 m
Smoothlands to Hartland Point 8.1 to 9.1 49 m 49 m
Inland lanes past Blagdon and Blegberry to Berry 9.1 to 11.7 105 m 93 m
Down to the Abbey River and up to Stoke 11.7 to 13.2 73 m 70 m

Figures come from the route's own waypoint data in OS Maps. Summed stretch by stretch they come to about 628 m up and down, a little more than the route's headline 600 m, because of how OS smooths the overall profile. The 3.5 km from the Quay to Smoothlands is the hardest part of the day, with about 260 m of climbing.
